inputs.source: On call engineer's chat request (SSO authenticated)

instructions.note: The prompt instructs the agent to deploy or run migrations on request and explicitly says not to ask for confirmation, which removes a natural check before sensitive production actions.

controls.name: Only on call engineers can access the assistant
controls.decay_rationale: Access control is enforced outside the model and does not weaken as model capability changes.

controls.name: Cloud audit logging of production actions
controls.decay_rationale: Logging remains available as a detective control unless removed, but it does not prevent misuse or fix attribution if all actions appear under the engineer's identity.

controls.name: Chat transcript retained as the only request record
controls.decay_rationale: Transcript retention is outside the model, but because engineers can delete their own history it does not provide durable attribution.

controls.name: Separate non-human agent identity for production actions
controls.decay_rationale: A separate service identity does not decay with model capability and would preserve actor attribution in logs.

controls.name: Immutable request and approval record bound to each production action
controls.decay_rationale: An append-only action record outside user-controlled chat history does not decay with model capability and would preserve non-repudiation.

findings.title: Shared human identity and deletable request record weaken attribution for production deploys and migrations

attack_path.note: Trusted on-call engineer request triggers action.
Agent can deploy to production using the engineer's personal token.
Agent can run irreversible production migrations using the same engineer identity.
Actions are logged only under the engineer's name.
The only request context is deletable chat history.

evidence.observation: The agent uses the on call engineer's personal access token, and every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name.
The only record of what the agent was asked, and why it acted, is the chat transcript, and engineers can delete their own chat history.
The prompt tells the agent to deploy services or run migrations when asked and to avoid asking for confirmation, increasing the chance that later disputes rely entirely on attribution records.
Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically, so disputed actions can have lasting operational impact.

recommendations.action: Execute production actions under a distinct agent or broker identity while preserving the requesting engineer identity as linked metadata in the audit record.
Create an immutable request-to-action record that binds prompt, parameters, timestamps, and resulting production action ids outside user-deletable chat history.

forecast.watch_signal: Any config or product change that removes cloud audit logging, shortens transcript retention, or increases unattended production actions should trigger reassessment.

rating.rationale: One present finding was identified. Trusted engineer input reaches S3 production configuration capability because production migration is irreversible, giving inherent moderate under the rubric. Declared controls are access restriction and detective logging/transcript retention; detective controls do not reduce tier, so residual remains moderate. Forecast remains moderate because the existing issue is a design-time attribution gap rather than a tier-increasing decay scenario. Manual validation was applied because scripts could not be run.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No source code, IaC, or runtime enforcement configuration was provided, so the assessment cannot verify how tokens are injected, how logs are bound to action ids, or whether transcript deletion is soft-delete versus permanent removal.
No separate tool manifest was provided; production action semantics were inferred from the prompt and runtime notes.
